title: Black Thursday, 1929 — the crash, and the 'White Knight' who tried to stop it
sources: Wikipedia: Wall Street crash of 1929 — on 24 October 1929, 'Black Thursday', the market lost 11% of its value at the opening bell; a record 12.9 million shares were traded; the volume left the ticker tape in brokerage offices hours behind, so investors had no idea what most stocks were trading for; on 29 October, 'Black Tuesday', some 16 million shares were traded; the crash cascaded into the worldwide Great Depression, though scholars disagree about its role

Wikipedia: Richard Whitney (financier) — on Black Thursday leading bankers (including Thomas Lamont of Morgan and Albert Wiggin of Chase) chose Whitney, vice-president of the Exchange, to act for them; he went onto the floor and ostentatiously bid for 25,000 shares of U.S. Steel at $205, well above the market, then made similar bids for other blue chips; it halted the slide that day, and earned him the name 'White Knight of Wall Street'; the respite was temporary; in 1938 he was charged with embezzlement, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to five to ten years in Sing Sing
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 2003 Concorde makes its last commercial flight; 1945 the United Nations comes into existence

Photos (public domain): crowds outside the New York Stock Exchange, 24 October 1929; brokers at the Exchange, 25 October 1929; a crowd after the crash, 29 October 1929; the trading floor after the crash, 1929; The New York Times, 30 October 1929; Richard Whitney before a Senate committee, 1937 (Harris & Ewing)
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a rotary telephone, turning pages

post.facebook:
On this day in 1929 — Black Thursday — the New York Stock Exchange lost 11 percent of its value at the opening bell.

A record 12.9 million shares changed hands. The ticker tape fell hours behind, so investors across the country had no idea what their stocks were worth. Crowds filled Wall Street.

The leading bankers met and sent in Richard Whitney, vice-president of the Exchange. In front of the traders, he bid for 25,000 shares of U.S. Steel at $205 — well above the market — then did the same with other blue-chip stocks. The slide stopped, and the papers called him the "White Knight of Wall Street".

It didn't last. On Black Tuesday, 29 October, the market collapsed. And the White Knight? In 1938 he was convicted of embezzlement and sent to Sing Sing.

youtube.description:
Black Thursday, 24 October 1929: the New York Stock Exchange lost 11% at the opening bell, a record 12.9 million shares traded, and the ticker tape fell hours behind. The bankers sent Richard Whitney onto the floor, where he bid for 25,000 shares of U.S. Steel far above the market price — and the slide stopped. He became the "White Knight of Wall Street". It didn't last: then came Black Tuesday. Nine years later, Whitney went to Sing Sing for embezzlement.
